modules.title: Code engineering with AI
modules.subtitle: Planning: from idea to MVP brief
modules.description: Learn to frame a narrow MVP task and fill a clear brief before Cursor.

content.whyBenefit: After this module you will have a clear MVP brief – who, what, and the limits for building with AI.
content.heroSubText: Prompt foundations – Modules 1–6. Here vibe coding = fast building with AI, but a narrow brief first before Cursor generation.
content.firstActionCTA: In 2 min write one user and one problem for your idea (first step; value and 1 feature come later). Or use the daily-priorities example.
outcomes: Must / Won’t and a testable success criterion
content.audience: For business and product people – a working prototype without deep programming.
content.footer: Next – slide 2: What you will do today

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Today: 1 problem, 1 user, 1 main feature, and a quick way to check if the prototype works. The result is not a presentation.

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body:
Pick an idea (e.g. a daily-priorities tool) and write one sentence: who you help and what you solve.

Example: “A manager doesn’t know where to start in the morning → 3 priorities.”
Template: [Who] cannot [do what] when [situation].

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Can you explain the task in 20 seconds without saying “app”?

slides.title: Stack map
slides.subtitle: Which layer when – not a tool fair

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Today you only plan. You will write code in Module 18 with Cursor (an AI coding editor). Leave hosting alone.

sections.heading: Stack layers
sections.body: Not Lovable/Replit as the main path in this course – brief now, code later with Cursor.

rows: You write the brief and critique
Optional: install; do not generate the whole app
You will need to show a result (M18)

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: Write down: brief now; Cursor install optional; generate – not today.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Are you already putting a tech stack in the brief? (You should not.)

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: We go: problem → person → value → 1 feature → brief → check. Code is Module 18.

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Bad: “I want an app with AI.” Good: a concrete user problem in a situation with a consequence.

sections.heading: Bad vs good start
sections.body: Start from the person, not the technology.

rows: “A manager spends 20 minutes sorting tasks in the morning and still starts with the wrong one.”
Focus – situation and consequence (wastes the morning / the team waits)

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: Rewrite your idea: who hurts, when, and what business/personal consequence.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Is the sentence about a person, not about technology?

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Formula: [User] faces [problem] when [situation], so [consequence]. Payments are not required in this MVP.

sections.heading: Filled example
sections.body: A manager faces priority chaos when the morning starts with email, so they waste 20 minutes and the team waits.

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: Fill the template: [User] faces [problem] when [situation], so [consequence].

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Is the problem frequent? Is the pain clear? Can a prototype check at least one part?

content.footer: Next – slide 7: Value is not a feature

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Value = change for the person (e.g. saves 10 min). Feature = action in the product (e.g. ranks 3 tasks).

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body:
Write a pair: value + feature in one sentence each.

Example: value – “knows where to start”; feature – “ranks 3 tasks”.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Does the value still make sense if you swapped the tool?

recognitionExercise.title: Spot it: value or feature?
recognitionExercise.task: Read 4 phrases and for each choose – **value** or **feature**.
examples: The person knows where to start, without stress.
explanations: Change for the person – that is value, not a button.
Reminder – a feature; value would be “doesn’t forget to start”.
recognitionExercise.goal: Value still makes sense if you swap the tool; a feature is a concrete product action.

slides.title: MVP scope
slides.subtitle: Must now · Can later · Won’t build

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Three columns: Must now / Can later / Won’t build. For the first MVP – 1 main feature (+ at most 1–2 helpers).

sections.heading: Triage zones
sections.body: Later in the brief – Must / Should / Won’t (same zones in English).

rows: Useful, but does not block the first test
Too early or too wide for the first MVP

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body:
Drop 5 of your ideas into the three columns (Must now / Can later / Won’t build).
Example (daily priorities): Must now – Top 3; Can later – reminder; Won’t build – login, payments, admin.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Does “Must now” fit into one short user cycle?

content.title: Creation card – 5 fields written down
content.body: Write in Docs or a notebook. Mark here when all 5 fields are written – that bridges to the brief.

sections.heading: Example (daily priorities)
sections.body:
1. User: a manager who assigns team tasks in the morning.
2. Problem: spends 20 minutes sorting and still starts with the wrong one.
3. Value: knows Top 3 in 2 minutes – the team does not wait.
4. Main feature: rank 3 daily tasks.
5. How we know it works: in 2 minutes the person sees Top 3.

sections.heading: 1. User
sections.body: Who uses it and in what context?

sections.heading: 2. Problem
sections.body: Concrete problem (not “I want an app”).

sections.heading: 3. Value created
sections.body: What changes for the user – not a feature list.

sections.heading: 4. Main feature
sections.body: One main feature (+ at most 1–2 helpers).

sections.heading: 5. How we know it works
sections.body: A testable success criterion (e.g. “In 2 minutes the person sees Top 3.”).

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Is there really one feature? Is the success criterion testable?

content.title: Card ready
content.subtitle: Next you will sharpen the idea and write the brief (one document). Still not code.
content.celebrationText: Great! 5 card fields – bridge to the brief. Checklist: user · problem · value · 1 feature · how you know it works.

nextSteps: Three brief maturity steps (Vibe → Skeleton → Refinement).

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: First lock the direction (Vibe – the feel of the idea), then the frame – cycle and bounds (Skeleton), then sharpen the brief (Refinement). This is not a second product path – only brief maturity.

sections.heading: Brief maturity steps
sections.body: Vibe → Skeleton → Refinement. Tap a rung.
sections.imageAlt: Brief maturity steps: Vibe, Skeleton, Refinement

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: Say: my idea is now at Vibe / Skeleton / Refinement – and why in one sentence.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Do you already have a cycle before polishing the text?

slides.title: Product sentence
slides.subtitle: One line – for whom and why

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: I build [product] that helps [person] solve [problem], giving [result].

sections.heading: Bad vs good
sections.body:
Bad: “I build an AI app for priorities.”
Good: “I build a daily-priorities tool that helps a manager see Top 3 fast, giving clarity in 2 minutes.”

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: Fill the formula from your 5 fields.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Does the sentence fit on one line?

content.footer: Next – slide 13: Three pillars and critique

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Three pillars: problem, user, value. Then critique – the sentence should get narrower.

sections.heading: Three pillars (from the card)
sections.body:
• Problem: morning priority chaos
• User: manager
• Value: Top 3 in 2 minutes

sections.heading: Before / After
sections.body:
Before: “I build an AI app for priorities for everyone.”
After: “I build a narrow tool for a manager – Top 3 daily priorities in 2 minutes.”

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: Run the Skeptic prompt on your idea and write After next to it.

sections.heading: Skeptic
sections.body: Copy and adapt to your context.
sections.copyable:
You are a skeptical product consultant. My idea: [briefly].
1) Find untested assumptions.
2) Ask at most 5 questions that reduce risk.
3) Say what is most likely to fail in the first prototype.
Do not suggest extra features or a tech stack.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Did the After sentence drop at least one assumption?

preCopyCheckBlock.question: Before copying the Skeptic – what must it not do?
options: Suggest extra features and a tech stack
Add Auth and Stripe as Must
Rewrite the whole product from scratch
preCopyCheckBlock.explanation: The Skeptic narrows assumptions – it does not add features or stack.

slides.title: Three directions
slides.subtitle: A / B / C – who, what, result

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Three narrow directions for the same problem – not 30 features.

sections.heading: Three directions A / B / C
sections.body: Example (daily priorities). Below – your own A/B/C.

rows: Knows where to start in 1 minute

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: Rewrite 3 lines for your idea (for whom / what it does / result).

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Is each direction still the same problem?

content.footer: Next – slide 15: Pick the most testable

slides.title: Pick the most testable
slides.subtitle: Pick the most testable direction in the lab

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Pick the direction you can validate fastest – not the prettiest. Scores are a guide, not an exam.

sections.heading: Direction lab
sections.body: Pick A, B, or C. After you pick you see scores and can copy why.
sections.imageAlt: Direction picker lab: A/B/C, scores, and copyable why

sections.heading: Guide 1–5 (example)
sections.body: Three criteria in plain language: (1) Speed to test – can you try it in a day? (2) Clarity – does the user get it without a lecture? (3) Risk – how much complexity (1 = low).

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: Pick A/B/C in the lab. Write the winner next to your card.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Is the winner testable in a day, not in a quarter?

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Describe how a person goes from need to result – 5 steps. This is not a feature list.

sections.heading: User cycle
sections.body: Trigger → input → action → result → next (with a loop back). Tap a step.
sections.imageAlt: User cycle with a return loop

sections.heading: Filled cycle (daily priorities)
sections.body:
1. Trigger: morning, need to know Top 3.
2. Input: enters 3–5 tasks.
3. Action: the system ranks them.
4. Result: sees Top 3.
5. Next: starts with the first / returns tomorrow.

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: Empty template for your winning direction: Trigger → Input → Action → Result → Next.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Is “Result” visible to the user in under 2 minutes? (Fast check = lower risk.)

content.footer: Next – slide 17: Screens from the flow

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Each screen = a cycle step. Max 3–5 – otherwise the MVP is too wide.

sections.heading: Screen ← cycle step
sections.body: Example (daily priorities) – max 5.

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: List screens from your cycle (≤5).

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Does each screen have a place in the cycle?

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: The same three columns in brief language: Must (≤4) = Must now · Should = Later · Won’t = Won’t. “Now” = one short cycle – not a quarterly plan.

sections.heading: Must / Should / Won’t and NNL
sections.body: Example for a daily-priorities tool – rewrite for your idea.

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body:
Fill the brief fields: Must (≤4) / Should / Won’t (≥3) and Now→Next→Later.
Example: Must – Top 3 in under 2 min; Should – reminder after the first check; Won’t – login / payments.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Are login/payments Won’t if they do not carry the first cycle?

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Three risks + how you will reduce them. Not a wide risk matrix – one line each.

sections.heading: 3 risks
sections.body: Examples – rewrite for your idea.

rows: Put in 3 sample tasks before the first try
Success criterion <2 min in the first cycle

sections.heading: Check

content.footer: Next – slide 20: Ready check before the brief

questions.question: Does “Must now” (Must) fit into ≤4 points in the first MVP brief?
options: No – you need ≥10 so you forget nothing
Must is only the tech stack
questions.explanation: Narrow brief: Must ≤4. If wrong – go back to “Bounds and Now–Next–Later”.

questions.question: What separates value from a feature?
options: Value = change for the user; feature = action in the product
Value and feature are the same
Value = how many screens you have
questions.explanation: Value = change; feature = how the product acts. See “Value is not a feature”.

questions.question: Do you have a 5-step flow (not a feature list)?
options: Yes – trigger → input → action → result → next
A feature list without a flow is enough
A flow is only needed after GitHub
questions.explanation: The cycle = UX sequence. See “User cycle”.

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: A brief is one document before code. Below are 11 fields. Stack and ERD are not here. You will use the same document in the Module 18 project.

sections.heading: 11 brief fields
sections.body:
1. Product sentence
2. Problem
3. Target user
4. Value promise
5. Main user cycle
6. MVP bounds (Must / Should / Won’t)
7. Main screens (≤5)
8. Data (high-level; detailed model – M18)
9. Now → Next → Later
10. 3 risks
11. Success criterion

sections.heading: Do this now
sections.body: Create a Docs file `01_MVP_BRIEF.md` (or a notebook page). Fill all 11. If stuck – use the Brief helper.

sections.heading: Brief helper
sections.body: Copy and adapt to your context.
sections.copyable:
Help me write a narrow MVP brief in English.
Context: [card / idea].
Rules: Must ≤4; Won’t ≥3; at most 3 gap questions; no tech stack (stack comes later).
Return 11 fields:
1) product sentence
2) problem
3) user
4) value
5) cycle
6) Must/Should/Won’t
7) screens ≤5
8) data (high-level)
9) Now→Next→Later
10) 3 risks
11) success criterion.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Must≤4? Won’t≥3? Success criterion testable in under 2 minutes?

briefCheckBlock.question: Which brief field is missing if you cannot say whether the MVP “works” in under 2 minutes?
briefCheckBlock.explanation: Without a testable success criterion the brief stays an idea. Stack and roadmap come later.

preCopyCheckBlock.question: Before copying the Brief helper – what is required in an MVP brief?
options: Must ≤4, Won’t ≥3, a testable success criterion
At least 10 screens and a full ERD
Only a product sentence with no bounds
preCopyCheckBlock.explanation: Narrow brief: Must/Won’t and a success criterion. Auth/payments are usually Won’t for the first MVP.

modules.title: Knowledge check (Code path)
modules.subtitle: Quiz: brief and planning quality
modules.description: Check that your brief is narrow and testable. ≥70% recommended before Module 18.

slides.title: Module 17 quiz
slides.subtitle: Brief and planning knowledge – not code

content.whyBenefit: After the quiz you will know whether your brief is narrow and testable enough before a Cursor project.
content.firstActionCTA: Answer questions about the brief and planning – not about code or deploy.
content.microWinPhrase: Each correct answer shows you can narrow the task before generation.
content.thresholdExplanation: When you reach ≥70%, you can move to Module 18 (project). If less – review Module 16 brief and triage slides.

questions.question: What is the best 1+1+1 start for an MVP task?
options: User + problem + 1 main feature (and a success criterion)
A list of 10 features + stack choice
“Build an app with AI” with no user
questions.explanation: A narrow start = person, problem, one feature. Stack and payments come later.

questions.question: Which statement is value, not a feature?
options: Saves 10 minutes in the morning lining up priorities
questions.explanation: Value = change for the person. The rest are features or infra.

questions.question: After the quiz, what will you do first in Module 18?
options: Assemble a BUILD PACKET (file pack before AI code: brief, flow, rules, Cursor prompt) – not “build the whole app”
Ask AI to write the whole system with no PACKET
Skip the brief and jump to multi-agent setup
Start with a Heroku blue-green course
questions.explanation: M18 axis: brief → PACKET (file pack) → Cursor slice → proof. Not chaotic generate.

testQuestions.question: Which start is bad?
options: A concrete user problem with a situation
testQuestions.explanation: Without a problem – only a technology wish.

testQuestions.question: “Ranks 3 tasks” – what is that?
testQuestions.explanation: That is a product action = feature. Value would be a time / stress change.

testQuestions.question: Auth and Stripe in the first MVP triage – where?
options: Can later or Won’t (Won’t for the first cycle)
testQuestions.explanation: Payments/auth are rarely required for the first narrow cycle.

testQuestions.question: Order the brief maturity phases Vibe → Skeleton → Refinement (first to last):
testQuestions.explanation: Vibe (feel of the idea) → Skeleton (cycle + bounds) → Refinement (sharpening).

testQuestions.question: What is usually missing in a weak brief?
testQuestions.explanation: Bounds and a testable Done – the brief core.

testQuestions.question: What better describes UX?
testQuestions.explanation: The cycle describes the user experience.

testQuestions.question: What is “too early” before a narrow MVP?
testQuestions.explanation: Infra and width without a first cycle – too early.

testQuestions.question: What should you give Cursor before generate?
options: PACKET (file pack) / rules / a vertical slice – context before generate

testQuestions.question: What is a good success criterion in an MVP brief?
options: In 2 minutes you can check that the main feature works for the user
“It will be modern” with no measure
10 screens and Auth as the first step
testQuestions.explanation: Success criterion = quickly testable Done, not fashion or infra.

testQuestions.question: MCP servers in the brief phase?
options: Too early for the core – not required
testQuestions.explanation: MCP/Spec Kit – not a required path in this course.

testQuestions.question: After an AI change – when do you read the diff?
options: Before commit: read the diff, then a quick check (smoke), then commit
Not needed if the UI “looks fine”
testQuestions.explanation: Diff ritual: status → diff → quick check (smoke) → commit → push. Details in Module 18.

slides.title: Results
slides.subtitle: Is the brief ready for Module 18?

content.passedMessage: Well done! Your brief looks narrow enough – you can go to the Module 18 project.
content.failedMessage: Worth revisiting Module 16: the 5-field card, triage (Must now / Can later / Won’t), the user cycle, and 01_MVP_BRIEF.md.
content.thresholdExplanation: When you reach ≥70%, you can move to Module 18. If less – review brief bounds, Value ≠ feature, and Vibe → Skeleton → Refinement.

useCaseBlock.heading: Next step: Module 18
useCaseBlock.body: If ≥70% – go to the project: assemble a BUILD PACKET (file pack before AI code), make one Cursor slice, and collect a soft DoD (lightweight proof – Module 18). If less – return to the card and brief in Module 16.

sections.copyable:
Stack: Cursor-first; do not change stack without asking.
Must: [1–4 points from the brief].
Won’t: [auth / payments / … – not in this MVP].
Done: [how we know it works].
Language: EN in UI copy; code – clear names.
Security: no keys in code or prompts.
Before a larger change: file plan → my “yes” → then code.

slides.title: Edge and .env
slides.subtitle: Normal / Edge / Error · no keys in prompts

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Edge cases: Normal / Edge / Error. Real keys – never in a committed .env on GitHub, never in prompts.

sections.heading: Pick a leak path
sections.body: Three paths – Bad|Good opens after you pick. Examples use PLACEHOLDER only (not a real key).

toolChoiceBar.question: Where do keys leak most often?
toolChoiceBar.sequenceHint: Pick a type – you will see Bad vs Good.

choices.label: Git
choices.pushSignal: The key ends up in repo history.
choices.badExample: API_KEY=sk-live-EXAMPLE_NOT_REAL in a file that goes into Git

choices.label: Prompt
choices.pushSignal: The key ends up in chat history or logs.
choices.badExample: Here is my key sk-live-EXAMPLE_NOT_REAL – add it to the fetch header.

choices.label: Commit
choices.pushSignal: Secret files enter the commit without a check.
choices.badExample: git add . && git commit -m "fix" – without status and diff

sections.heading: Copy the good – Git
sections.body: Use .env.example without real keys.
sections.copyable:
.env – gitignore.
.env.example:
API_KEY=YOUR_API_KEY_HERE
# PLACEHOLDER – not a real key

sections.heading: Copy the good – Prompt
sections.body: Ask for an env variable – do not show the key.
sections.copyable:
Use process.env.API_KEY (or the matching env).
Do not paste the key value into the prompt and do not commit .env.

sections.heading: Copy the good – Commit
sections.body: Before commit – status and diff.
sections.copyable:
Before commit:
1) git status – is .env absent?
2) git diff – no sk- / API_KEY= real values?
Only then commit.

sections.heading: In short
sections.body: Before a larger AI change – commit a working version. After AI: read the diff, then a quick check (smoke), then commit.

sections.heading: Diff ritual
sections.body: Status → **diff** → quick check (smoke) → commit → push. Tap a step – diff is emphasized.

recognitionExercise.title: Recognize the diff ritual order
recognitionExercise.task: Read 4 situations and pick which step is missing or out of order.
examples: After an AI change, commit + push immediately with no reading.
Before a larger AI change there is no commit of a working version.
Read the diff, ran smoke, then commit.
Pushed before smoke because they “were in a hurry”.
choices: Missing: read the diff before commit
Missing: commit a working version before AI
explanations: Diff comes before commit – otherwise you risk a blind AI diff.
Safe start: commit a working state before a larger AI change.
status → diff → smoke → commit → push – teisinga seka.
Smoke before push – otherwise you would break the remote branch.
